issues.issue: Unlike the parallel City representation in Section 6.A, this one omits "delivery" from the dates on which authorization is warranted, and it names no corporate act or officer as the source of authorization. The asymmetry invites argument about what Hardrives actually warranted.

The covenant to "lay no waste" and to surrender the Premises "in as good a condition as received" is hard to square with Section 2, which contemplates industrial production, distribution and sale of paving materials and storage of heavy equipment on the site. What counts as waste, and what baseline condition was "received," are set by two provisions pulling apart.

"A policy of insurance in the amount of $1,000,000.00 to include comprehensive liability coverage" does not say whether the figure is per occurrence or aggregate, nor what other coverages the policy must "include." The required insurance cannot be measured from the words used.

The duty to use "all precautions necessary to ensure against the creation, use, or storage of any hazardous material or waste on the Premises" cannot readily be reconciled with the Section 2 use provisions permitting production of paving materials and storage of all equipment and supplies necessary for that purpose. One provision permits what the other requires be prevented.

"Environmental Protection Agency laws or regulations" is an inexact term: the EPA promulgates regulations but does not enact laws, and the phrase does not say whether the Ohio EPA and state requirements are included. Its coverage is left to construction.

The hold-harmless covers "any and all claims, liabilities, damages, and losses ... resulting from injury on or about the Premises" without saying whether it reaches claims arising from the City's own conduct or from conditions existing before the license. "Injury" is also unqualified as to whether it includes property and environmental harm as well as personal injury.

Read literally, the indemnity would shift back to Hardrives losses caused by breach of the City's environmental warranties in Section 6.D, which Section 8 expressly preserves. The two provisions cannot both be given full effect as to pre-existing contamination.

"All work performed on the Premises" does not define "work" or say by whom it must be performed, so its reach over ordinary operations, construction, and third-party contractors is unclear. It also overlaps a narrower compliance duty in Section 7.D without saying which governs.

The "as is" acceptance without express or implied warranty stands against the City's affirmative environmental and title warranties in Sections 6.B and 6.D, which the carve-out purports to save. Whether "as is" bars a claim over the condition of the Premises, or the Section 6 warranties survive it, is precisely the question the two provisions leave open.

The integration clause makes this Agreement and "the documents delivered pursuant hereto" the entire understanding, but Section 5 makes the parties' rights turn on a Development Agreement to be entered into later. Whether the contemplated Development Agreement is inside or outside the integrated whole is unresolved.

"A duly authorized written instrument" does not identify who must authorize an amendment on the City's side, whether the Board of Control alone or City Council as referenced in Section 6.A. The authorization standard is left undefined.

The bar on assignment without written consent sits against Section 12, which declares that "City" and "Hardrives" include their successors and assigns. Whether the Agreement runs to assigns, or cannot be assigned at all absent consent, is left for construction.

The survival clause says warranties and covenants "survive the execution and delivery" of the Agreement but says nothing about survival after expiration of the one-year term or termination under Section 4. How long the City's Section 6 warranties remain enforceable is not fixed by these words.

Extending "City" and "Hardrives" to "successors, and assigns" conflicts with Section 9, which makes the Agreement not assignable by either party without written consent. The two sentences give inconsistent answers to whether an assignee holds rights under the license.

The Premises "shall include, but is not limited to," Parcel No. 3 of the LTV quit-claim deed, so the very exhibit meant to fix the licensed property expressly declines to bound it. Nothing else in the instrument identifies what else the Premises includes.

This metes-and-bounds description makes Parcel No. 3 a 58.086-acre tract, while the Environmental Site Assessment attached as Exhibit B and referenced in Section 6.D describes "Parcel No. 3" as a 5.44-acre site. The identity of the parcel the environmental disclosures cover cannot be settled without reconciling the two exhibits.

The three carve-outs are taken from Parcel No. 3 as described, yet the opening sentence of Exhibit A says the Premises is "not limited to" that parcel, so it is unclear whether the exceptions limit the Premises as a whole. Their effect also has to be read against the Section 6.B warranty that the Premises are clear of liens and claims.
